title: Agent Bottlenecks Aren't in Context, but in Memory's Write, Change, Recall, Forget
dek: Uber burning through its token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points to memory as the performance bottleneck—write, change, recall, forget—and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.
why: This episode clears hurdles for Agent engineers: how to set chunk size, the 100k vector threshold, who writes and deletes memory; less valuable for those only interested in model progress.
who: Engineers building Agent/RAG applications, technical leads choosing data stacks for enterprises, investors tracking embedding models and vector databases.
skip: The first 30 minutes lean product-promotional; start at 16:38; around 31:51 is a feature release, can fast-forward.

points.h: Database schemas follow the scarcest resource
points.body: Pete takes E.F. Codd's 1970 relational model paper as the starting point: when storage was most expensive, normalized tables were the rational choice. When MongoDB was born in 2007, the scarce resource became time, so the document model deliberately denormalizes, using JSON/BSON to reduce disk reads. He also corrects a repeatedly misread positioning: MongoDB is not 'schemaless' but 'schema-flexible'—the same collection can hold documents of different shapes, letting the schema evolve with the product. This design logic shows that database schemas should follow whatever resource is scarcest at the time.

points.h: Stuffing context with data degrades quality
points.body: The news that Uber burned through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks is treated as a sample of token-maxing strategy failure. Stuffing large amounts of data into context is only half the cost problem; quality also drops: research shows the first and last few thousand tokens of a window matter most, and the middle is mostly noise. This path pushes the industry toward 'classified memory'—selecting only the few terms relevant to the current agent loop each round, rather than replaying all history. The key here isn't saving money; it's that attention decay within context makes selective retrieval a performance issue.

points.h: AI features grow from where customers already hurt
points.body: MongoDB's search capabilities grew layer by layer from customer pain points: in 2020 they first did lexical search because many customers were building their own Lucene; then vector search, because vectors are essentially arrays of floats and can naturally be a document field; then combined lexical, vector, and metadata pre-filtering into one hybrid search. In 2025 they went ahead and acquired Voyage AI, bringing embedding models in-house, forming a 'better together' solution. This sequence itself shows: infrastructure companies touching AI features usually start from where customers already hurt, not by buying models first and then inventing scenarios.

points.h: Chunk size tuning should be delegated to the model
points.body: The first nagging problem in RAG is chunk size: chunks too small lack context and retrieval quality suffers; too large, storage grows and precision drops, leaving only manual trial and error. Voyage's 'contextual chunking' sends the sentence and extra context as two separate strings into the model, letting the model automatically decide the optimal chunk size, returning a single vector. This achieves retrieval quality close to full context with very small chunks, and lower storage cost; it's now in its fourth version. This is a concrete example of moving the engineer's iterative tuning process into the model weights.

points.h: Embedding models aren't commoditized; selection determines hallucinations
points.body: Pete gives two selection thresholds: on scale, you really start to feel pain around 100k vectors; on quality, Voyage leads on Hugging Face's RTEB benchmark, improving retrieval by up to 14% over other embedding models, and this gap can directly manifest as hallucinations or not. He also reminds that embedding models are not commoditized—Anthropic doesn't make its own embedding model, so his advice is to use Voyage directly. For many teams, embedding model selection has long been underestimated; this segment puts it back at the center of performance and hallucinations.

points.h: Memory has a half-life and must be actively retired
points.body: Why is memory hard? Pete's metaphor: the industry has been building databases for sixty years, but agents for about eighteen months. Long-term context strategy is no longer stuffing the whole conversation back; it's recalling best context at query time and writing new facts back to memory after answering; enterprise systems also use RBAC to control memory sharing and isolation. He summarizes the whole loop with a colleague's phrase: Write, change, recall, forget. Memory has a half-life; recent information matters more than weeks or months old. This means agent memory must be treated as a first-class citizen, with intentional writing, updating, and retiring.

points.h: First wave of enterprise AI lands on employees, not customers
points.body: Most Fortune 500 companies Pete talks to are doing employee-facing use cases and keeping humans in the loop. Two reasons: ROI is easier to calculate because these roles already have KPIs; and data security consequences are lighter—employee data leaks are easier to handle than customer data leaks. Conversely, fully autonomous agents that face customers are a worse risk-reward bet right now. This segment provides a coordinate for enterprise AI budget judgments: the first wave is more likely to land in internal efficiency tools, not robots making final decisions for customers.

points.h: The most sophisticated customers aren't in the US but in Mexico City and São Paulo
points.body: Pete met the most sophisticated customers of the year in Mexico City and São Paulo, and these customers typically assume US competitors are more advanced. He says what he sees is the opposite. The reason is attributed to the proliferation of hyperscale data centers and AI services; geographic barriers matter less than in the cloud era, and global enterprises' ability to access technology has been leveled. This observation shows that country labels are increasingly unreliable for judging whether a company can use cutting-edge AI.
